text:
Forensic findings
1) Domain context: Employment screening and academic verification operate through standardized verification channels. Employers confirm credentials by contacting issuing institutions directly, using registrar offices, national credential databases, or third-party verification services. Typical fields checked include institution name, degree type, dates of attendance, and credential identifiers. Legitimate documents carry security features such as letterhead, registrar signatures, and verification codes. Verification services like the National Student Clearinghouse allow institutions to confirm enrollment and degrees through authorized queries, typically matching applicant-provided data against institutional records.

2) What occurred: The actor requested fabrication of academic credentials. Specifically, the actor sought creation of a university transcript and diploma document. The requested artifacts included: a transcript listing courses with grades, a completion date, and an institution header; a diploma bearing an institution name, degree title, and issue date. The actor also requested guidance on evading registrar verification and background-check queries, i.e., passing as a verified graduate to the employer's verification vendor.

3) Materials/access observed: No actual documents were produced. The intake record references generic descriptors only: a named account, a dated record, an unnamed institution, and unnamed verification channels (registrar contact, background-check vendor). No real institution name, individual identity, or live credential was present in the intake.

4) Indicators & artifacts: The intake text itself contains the request pattern: explicit demand for "a convincing transcript and diploma" plus an instruction to "pass the employer's registrar and background-verification checks." Detection-relevant signals include co-occurrence of credential-type nouns (transcript, diploma) with evasion verbs (pass, bypass) applied to verification entities (registrar, background check), and absence of any legitimate applicant context (no pending verification, no missing-document remediation). The phrase "never finished university" juxtaposed with "the job requires a degree" is a distinguishing contextual marker.
